headline: High-risk filesystem/network asymmetry: xonsh can write and exfiltrate while spring-integration-samples has no runtime isolation or egress controls documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, so prompt injection is not default. However, agent_b can read/write files and use stdin/stdout, while agent_a is a code sample repo with no isolation details; if outputs are manually copied or file-shared, injected content could be misread as instructions. The pathway is weaker than data leakage but plausible.
conditions: IF operator copies agent_a output into files or stdin consumed by agent_b, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared workspace is introduced, agent_b may parse attacker-controlled content as commands.
mitigations: Keep agents on separate workspaces.
Avoid copy-pasting untrusted text into shell sessions.
Use explicit delimiters for any transferred content.
Review file inputs before agent_b consumes them.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b has broad network egress and filesystem access, while agent_a has no network egress and no data classes touched. The pair can still leak local files if agent_b is pointed at shared content or environment variables; agent_a does not add a second leak path. This is a default-capable exfiltration risk for agent_b, but not enough for high without sensitive data evidence.
conditions: IF agent_b is given access to sensitive files or environment variables, those contents can be transmitted off-host.
IF both agents share a workspace, agent_b can read and exfiltrate files created for agent_a.
mitigations: Restrict agent_b to a non-sensitive directory.
Unset secrets from the environment before running agent_b.
Block outbound network for agent_b when not needed.
Use separate OS users for each agent.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; agent_a is a repository of samples with no runtime write capability documented, but the pair still overlaps on filesystem interaction through shared files. Because agent_b lacks modify_git_state and supports only one instance, the conflict is narrower than the high indicator, yet concurrent writes to the same directory remain plausible.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, agent_b can overwrite files used by agent_a.
IF a git checkout is present and agent_b writes into it, file-state conflicts can occur even without git mutation.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Run only one agent per workspace.
Make shared directories read-only.
Snapshot files before agent_b writes to them.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b can execute shell commands and subprocesses, so if it consumes agent_a's outputs as instructions or configuration, errors can cascade into actions. agent_a is a samples repo, not a verified reasoning system, so its outputs are not authoritative; still, the pair creates a classic unverified-input-to-action path unless the operator inserts validation.
conditions: IF agent_a output is piped into agent_b commands, agent_b may act on incorrect assumptions.
IF operator uses agent_a-generated text as configuration for agent_b, downstream shell actions can be wrong.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Validate any generated commands against a dry run.
Separate planning output from execution input.
Log and inspect command diffs before running them.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either open-source agent, so compliance risk is limited. The only concrete issue is that agent_b can handle filesystem contents and environment variables while agent_a has no stated compliance controls; without a named regulated data class, this remains a low-confidence gap rather than a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in agent_b's filesystem or environment, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF a deployment requires retention or residency guarantees, neither profile documents them.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in both agents.
Document retention and deletion expectations.
Run a quick data-classification check before use.
Keep audit logs of any file transfers.
